The Method of Moments (MoM) system matrix Z is dense and scales as N² in fill time and storage, and N³ in LU factorization time.
Adaptive Cross Approximation (ACA) compresses off-diagonal blocks of Z and its LU factors into low rank outer product matrices.
Unknowns are grouped spatially using a cobblestone distance sorting technique based on geometric proximity.
Off-diagonal blocks of the impedance matrix and LU factors are compressible due to over-sampling of distant interactions.
Singular values of typical off-diagonal matrix blocks decay exponentially to machine precision within about 30 singular values out of over 200.
ACA requires only a few rows and columns of a matrix block to compute its low rank approximation, reducing operations count.
The LU factorization of the compressed matrix is performed directly using ACA without explicit full matrix fill.
The approach is validated on benchmark geometries such as SLICY and Open Pipe.
The method uses standard Rao-Wilton-Glisson (RWG) basis functions and Galerkin test functions, preserving matrix symmetry.
The ACA method compresses the right-hand side excitation vectors and current solution vectors for monostatic scattering.
Memory and runtime reductions achieved can be orders of magnitude compared to traditional MoM solutions.
The method enables solving problems with up to one million unknowns on inexpensive computer resources.
The matrix blocks are approximated as outer products of a column dominant matrix U and a row dominant matrix V, with rank k much smaller than block dimensions.
Error tolerance in low rank approximation is measured by the Frobenius norm of the difference between original and approximated matrices.
The diagonal blocks of the system matrix are not compressible and must be treated fully.
The ACA-based LU factorization avoids the convergence issues typical of iterative solvers for large, complex geometries.
The computational complexity for LU factorization grows as the sixth or ninth power of body size for surface or volume problems respectively without compression.
The ACA technique was introduced by Bebendorf and has been adapted here for direct LU factorization and solution.
The method does not require far/near field distinctions, auxiliary equivalent sources, or analytic Green's function expansions.
The paper includes detailed discussions of singular value decomposition theory to justify low rank approximations.
